decisions.reason: MemoryForge “synthesize[s] such lifelong memory from brief target personas” as a framework step, and the “frozen LLMs... dynamically retrieve situation-relevant memory” — the store is authored offline by MemoryForge, not written by the agent itself at run time, so T2 routes it to E3.

“an SLM agent actively organizes memory by clustering... autonomously generates cluster-specific profiles” and retrieves via a two-stage filter — the agent writes and reorganizes its own store at run time and reads it back, satisfying I1 via T2.

The method “post-processes model outputs and corrects factual inconsistencies via external semantic memory” built from RDF triples; there is no description of an agent writing to this store across turns, only single-shot retrieval-based correction, so T2 routes it to E3.

SkeMex runs “a closed-loop ‘Read–Write–Assess–Govern’ lifecycle... writing new skills, updating utilities, promoting useful memories, and removing harmful entries” for a medical agent, an explicit run-time write/retrieve mechanism conditioning future reasoning.

OCR-Memory “renders historical trajectories into images... retrieves stored experience via a locate-and-transcribe paradigm” — the agent's own run-time history is written and later retrieved to guide long-horizon behavior.

PerLTQA proposes “a novel framework for memory integration in QA, consisting of... Memory Classification, Memory Retrieval, and Memory Fusion” — a dataset/framework characterizing long-term memory capability, covered by T6.

The only memory mention is “enhancing their context-awareness and long-term memory” in a passing sentence; CMAT's actual contribution is adaptive weight-update tuning between agents, with memory neither named as a mechanism nor evaluated, so T5 applies.

Mem-Gallery is “a new benchmark for evaluating multimodal long-term conversational memory in MLLM agents” with “benchmarking across thirteen memory systems” — an evaluation methodology for agent memory, covered by T6.

The paper is “an independent reproducible testbed” comparing agent memory frameworks “mem0, Graphiti, and cognee... against retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and full-context baselines” — an evaluation study of agent memory systems (T6).

MemGraphRAG “employs a collaborative society of agents supported by shared memory, which provides a unified global context throughout the extraction process”, letting agents “dynamically resolve logical conflicts” — written/read shared multi-agent memory, T7.

MemVLN's “Episodic Memory management... applies pyramidal resolutions... concentrates computation on immediate percepts while retaining compressed long-term history” is an explicit policy over what survives into future navigation steps for an LLM-driven agent (T4).

POLAR “organizes prior interactions into a multimodal knowledge graph... retrieves relevant memories to interpret the current request and guide task execution” — an embodied MLLM agent writing and retrieving memory across long-term interactions (T2).

AutoMem lets the agent itself decide memory management: “a strong LLM reviews complete agent trajectories and iteratively revises the memory structure” and trains “the agent's own good memory decisions” — an agent-authored policy over what persists (T4).
The AFTER benchmark evaluates “how skills transfer across tasks, roles, and model backbones” for procedural memory in LLM agents — a benchmark/evaluation methodology for agent memory (T6).

TiMem builds a “Temporal Memory Tree... enabling systematic memory consolidation from raw conversational observations to progressively abstracted persona representations” — agent-written, consolidated memory retrieved across sessions (T2).

The method “continually compresses the accumulating attention key/value pairs into a compact memory space, facilitating language model inference in a limited memory space” — KV-cache compression for throughput/context handling, not cross-turn agent state (T1/E1).

HyperSkill maintains a hypergraph memory where “Periodic structure-informed maintenance prunes low-utility nodes and merges redundant skills via quality-weighted propagation” — the agent writes, evolves and retrieves its own skill memory (T2).
“This survey provides a capability-oriented review of personalized LLM-powered agents”, synthesizing existing methods into a taxonomy — an explicit secondary/aggregating study (D1/E4).

EgoSelf includes “a graph-based interaction memory constructed from past observations... from which user-specific profiles are derived” — the assistant writes interaction memory and retrieves it to condition future personalization (T2).

GAM “explicitly decouples memory encoding from consolidation... isolating ongoing dialogue in an event progression graph and integrating it into a topic associative network only upon semantic shifts” — explicit run-time memory write/consolidation for an LLM agent (T2).

PRE-Mem “extracts fine-grained memory fragments... then establishes explicit relationships between memory items across sessions” — memory is constructed at storage time and retrieved across sessions (T2).

Text2Mem “defines a compact yet expressive operation set aligned with encoding, storage, and retrieval” including “merge, promote, demote, split, lock, and expire” — a standardized run-time write/read interface for agent memory (T2).

“external memory” appears only once, inside a list of mutable modules (“foundational models, system prompts, tool-access policies, external memory”) supporting an identity/reputation argument; no memory mechanism is described or evaluated (T5).

“leveraging LLM capabilities, cognitive mechanisms, and contextual memory retrieval” is a passing description of the virtual-patient chatbot; the paper's actual contribution is the training tool and its usability score, memory is not named or evaluated (T5).

The whole abstract concerns “episodic memory in AI agents”, arguing it “will also introduce significant new risks” and proposing “four principles to guide the development of episodic memory capabilities” — a primary position piece squarely on the memory topic (T6).

Agents “play repeated games while retaining memory of previous interactions, including who played which roles and how they behaved”, and reference this in later statements — cross-session agent-written memory conditioning future behavior (T2).

AgentIR is built for “long-term conversational memory” where “the index grows during the query stream”, benchmarked on LongMemEval and LoCoMo — an engineering/evaluation study of agent memory retrieval (T6).

LUFY “focuses on emotionally arousing memories and retains less than 10% of the conversation... prioritizing arousing memories while forgetting the majority of the conversation” — an explicit policy over what conversational content persists across sessions (T4).

EMPO² requires “only a few trials with memory and no parameter updates” for out-of-distribution adaptation, implying memory persists across trials to guide exploration; the abstract underspecifies the write mechanism, so included per the uncertainty rule.

StreamMeCo “evict[s] the redundant memory nodes while maintaining the accuracy” and adds “a time-decay memory retrieval mechanism” — an explicit retention/eviction policy for a streaming vision agent's memory (T4).

The framework encodes failures as nodes/edges “forming a retrievable failure pattern subgraph” that agents “proactively retrieve” in later “task planning, tool calling, and multi-agent collaboration” — shared memory written and read across the multi-agent system (T7).

TALM's “long-term memory module enables semantic querying and integration of prior knowledge, supporting implicit self-improvement through experience reuse” for a multi-agent code-generation framework (T2).

The paper is about “Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for energy consumption forecasting” and hardware-accelerated ML for building management systems, with no LLM or agent described — positively not an LLM agent (D2/E6).

“acquire memory” is one item in a list of agent runtime capabilities (“Skills, synthesize tools, fork child processes... commit checkpoints”); the paper's actual focus is capability-controlled security admission, and memory is never elaborated as a contribution (T5).

The paper proposes “Governed Evolving Memory (GEM)”, replacing “record-level database operations with four state-level operators: ingestion, revision, forgetting, and retrieval” for long-term agent memory — a primary position paper squarely on memory design (T2).

The study is about context formatting/schema structure for SQL-generation tasks (“4 formats (YAML, Markdown, JSON, TOON)”); no memory or cross-turn/session state is described, only how much/what shape of context the model attends to (T4/E1).

SagaLLM “bridges this gap by integrating the Saga transactional pattern with persistent memory, automated compensation, and independent validation agents” — persistent memory is explicitly named as the mechanism enabling recovery/consistency across the workflow (T2).

SCOPE “routes guidelines between tactical memory (immediate error correction) and strategic memory, which is continuously refined through conflict resolution, subsumption pruning, and consolidation” to evolve the agent's own prompt (T4).

LatticeMind is “a conflict-aware structured memory that handles contradiction at write time. It maintains explicit item status” for multi-agent LLM systems — explicit run-time write/read memory conditioning multi-agent behavior (T7).

CAIM consists of “the Memory Controller as the central decision unit; the Memory Retrieval, which filters relevant data... and the Post-Thinking, which maintains the memory storage” for long-term human-AI interaction (T2).

“collaborative User and Item Memory Agents maintain persistent multimodal memories and update them through an attribute-guided reinforcement-and-reflection mechanism” — shared, agent-written memory across the multi-agent recommendation system (T7).

Lucid is “a black-box adversarial framework that compromises multimodal memory pipelines” via “Memory poisoning” and “Memory injection”, evaluated across “five black-box memory architectures” — an attack on agent memory (T6).

ComMem performs “test-time adaptation (TTA) of vision-language models” for classification via a visual cache and refined text prototypes across test samples; no agent, tool use, or task-taking behavior is described — positively not an LLM agent (D2/E6).

CMV “models session history as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with formally defined snapshot, branch, and trim primitives that enable context reuse across independent parallel sessions” — an explicit policy over what survives across sessions (T4).

The study examines “the relationship between interacting attention heads and human episodic memory”, directly comparing induction heads to “the contextual maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of human episodic memory” — human memory/neuroscience research is E6 per D2, not E5.

Mandol organizes memory into “a basic layer representing raw memory information and a high-level abstract layer that agglomerates basic memories into traceable abstract memories” for cross-session conversational agents (T2).
ChronoMem “commits whole-memory snapshots at each memory write, maintains structured version histories, and supports natural-language rollback requests” for LLM agent memory (T2).

A-MAC “decomposes memory value into five complementary and interpretable factors... and learns domain-adaptive admission policies” — an explicit run-time write-gating mechanism for LLM agent memory (T2).

E-mem has “multiple assistant agents maintain uncompressed memory contexts, while a central master agent orchestrates global planning” — multi-agent memory construction and retrieval across the reasoning process (T7).

“maintaining memory” is one item in a list of runtime responsibilities (“scheduling jobs, calling tools, maintaining memory, and pushing results to humans”, “a knowledge-base memory plane”); the paper's contribution is a failure taxonomy, not the memory mechanism (T5).

The paper proposes a theory of “memory consolidation” in “high-capacity neocortical networks” with “biologically plausible predictive coding circuits” — human/brain memory research, explicitly E6 per D2's neuroscience note.

EchoGuard runs a “structured Log-Analyze-Reflect loop: users log interactions, which the agent structures as nodes and edges in a personal, episodic KG... executes complex graph queries to detect... patterns” — agent-written/retrieved knowledge-graph memory (T2).
“Using a PRISMA-inspired framework, we systematically reviewed nearly 250 scholarly sources” — an explicit secondary/survey study of evaluation methods (D1/E4).

MemPO “enables the agent (policy model) to autonomously summarize and manage their memory during interaction with environment”, “selectively retain crucial information” — an agent-authored policy over what persists (T4).
“we propose a comprehensive survey on the memory of LLM-driven AI systems”, organizing prior work into a taxonomy — an explicit survey (D1/E4).

The framework has “a multi-agent architecture with actor, memory, and critic agents” enabling “automatic memory generation, reward annotation, and adaptive retrieval” with memory “managed through reward-based evaluation, merging, and pruning” (T2).

The paper studies how “bias propagates to future agents retrieving from the same memory store” across “four experimental phases” — characterizing a vulnerability of agent memory consolidation/retrieval systems (T6).

H2-LLM is a “Hybrid-bonding-based Heterogeneous accelerator” using “near-memory processing (NMP)” embedded in “DRAM dies” for low-batch LLM inference — hardware/DRAM memory optimization with no cross-turn agent state (T1/E1).

“the memory recollection mechanism for the dynamic execution agent” is a single unelaborated clause; the paper's actual contribution is a proactive-clarification planning framework (CEP), not the memory design (T5).

“we discuss work showing that these systems implement some key features of episodic memory” and “this article is part of the theme issue’Elements of episodic memory’” — a synthesizing review of existing AI systems to inform biological memory theory (D1/E4).
“This survey presents a comprehensive and structured synthesis of memory in LLMs and MLLMs, organizing the literature into a cohesive taxonomy” — an explicit survey (D1/E4).

The paper reports a “pre-registered recall experiment” and a “live” confirmatory study of a “memory palace” system that anchors and retrieves language-agent memories by world coordinate — a primary empirical study of agent memory read/write/recall (T2).

ExpeL “autonomously gathers experiences and extracts knowledge using natural language from a collection of training tasks. At inference, the agent recalls its extracted insights and past experiences” (T2).

The architecture comprises “six cognitive mechanisms: sleep-phase consolidation, interference-based forgetting, engram maturation, reconsolidation upon retrieval, entity knowledge graphs, and hybrid multi-cue retrieval” for LLM agents, evaluated on LongMemEval (T2).

MEMFLOW identifies “Memory Control Flow Attacks (MCFA)” where “memory can dominate the control flow, forcing unintended tool usage even against explicit user instructions” — an attack characterizing agent memory vulnerability (T6).

“Memory Decoder introduces a parametric long-term memory module” and studies “allocating more parameters to memory” — purely parametric memory with no externalized run-time store the agent itself writes to (T3/E2).

“the memoryless agents repeat wrong calls for days at a time” — the evaluated trading agents are explicitly memoryless; memory is only mentioned as motivating “a memory-aware, LLM-based successor”, i.e. future work, not the paper's contribution (T5).
The paper tunes “Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks... for wind power generation forecasting” — a neural time-series model, no LLM or agent in the loop (D2/E6).
DGAP targets “Emerging persistent memory technologies, such as Optane DCPMM” for dynamic graph analysis — a hardware persistent-memory systems paper with no agent state semantics (T1/E1).

SkillPCF is “a closed-loop agent framework that combines a physics-guided memory skill bank, reinforcement-learned skill selection, and simulator-grounded skill evolution” across iterative design trials (T2).

Warp Cortex “reduce[s] memory complexity from O(N * L) to O(1) for weights and O(N * k) for context” by treating “the KV-cache as a point cloud” — a GPU/VRAM memory-efficiency optimization for scaling agent count, not cross-session agent state (T1/E1).

The method “distills inference-time compute... into compact modular latent memories capturing the underlying reasoning structure. These memories are stored and retrieved for future inputs” while also being “trained with only a few gradient steps” — a hybrid of parametric update and externally stored/retrieved memory (T3).

True Memory “shifts the center of the system from a storage schema to a multi-stage retrieval pipeline operating over events preserved verbatim”, evaluated on LoCoMo, LongMemEval and BEAM-1M agent-memory benchmarks (T2).
ReMe performs “context-adaptive reuse... and utility-based refinement, which autonomously adds valid memories and prunes outdated ones” — an agent-managed procedural memory lifecycle (T2).
AMemGym is “an interactive environment enabling on-policy evaluation and optimization for memory-driven personalization” for LLM assistants — a benchmark for agent memory (T6).

The framework's “key innovation is a formal mechanism for agent memory evolution, where AI-driven self-reflection on past actions organically updates long-term characteristics, enabling the simulation of learned habits” (T2).
“This survey makes three contributions. First, we introduce a four-dimensional taxonomy, covering... memory architecture” applied to 12 systems — an explicit survey (D1/E4).

RFM-RAG “transforms the stateless retrieval of previous methods into stateful continuous knowledge management by constructing a dynamic evidence pool... Retrieves critical external knowledge to iteratively update this evidence pool” — run-time writes added to an otherwise classical RAG pipeline (T2).

SleepGate “augments transformer-based LLMs with a learned sleep cycle over the key-value (KV) cache”, including “a forgetting gate trained to selectively evict or compress stale cache entries” — within-context KV-cache management with no agent or cross-session persistence described (T1/E1).

The framework augments LLMs with “relational databases as external memory”, data that is “typically stored in relational databases” beforehand — classical retrieval over a fixed corpus, not content the agent writes at run time (T2/E3).

ASM “represents interaction sequences as a compact set of causally linked intermediate-state anchors to enable subgoal-targeted retrieval and attribution-aware decision making” for long-horizon GUI agents (T2).

The paper proposes a general “graph-augmented vector retrieval” technique for ANN search, applicable to “memory-augmented agents” among other uses, but describes no agent writing state — a static retrieval/embedding-selection method (T2/E3).

BitMar's decoder is “used to query a fixed-size key-value episodic memory” for image-text generation — retrieval over a bounded/fixed memory store, with no description of the model writing new entries during interaction (T2/E3).

This is a clinical drug trial: “Women with IIH... were treated with exenatide... or placebo”, measuring “episodic memory” as a human cognitive outcome — human medical research, no LLM or agent (D2/E6).
MemChain “transforms retrieved candidates into answer-facing active memory... executes explicit memory actions to produce a concise evidence context”, trained with reinforcement learning (T2).

“discussions centered on the agents' own architecture, especially memory, learning, and self-reflection, are prevalent in the corpus” — memory is a topic-modeling finding about agent discourse content, not the study's own memory mechanism (T5).

“This review connects ten historical cognitive architectures, eight language-agent runtime families, and forty-two mechanism-focused modern systems”, coding “evidence relation” across them — an explicit mechanism-level review (D1/E4).

The method “gradually distills episodic retrievals into parametric semantic memory” specifically to reduce “attention operations”/compute on GPT-2, an inference-efficiency technique, not cross-session agent state (T1/E1).

CTIM-Rover “extends agentic reasoning frameworks with an episodic memory, more specifically, a general and repository-level Cross-Task-Instance Memory (CTIM)” for software-engineering agents — a primary empirical study characterizing memory's effects (T2).

RMM integrates “Prospective Reflection, which dynamically summarizes interactions across granularities... into a personalized memory bank for effective future retrieval” and “Retrospective Reflection, which iteratively refines the retrieval” (T2).

M3Exam is a “query-centric multimodal conversational memory benchmark” and proposes “M3Proctor, a multimodal memory method that detects query modality bias and consumes raw visual sources only on demand” (T6).

EpMAN's “output of episodic attention is then used to reweigh the decoder's self-attention to the stored KV cache of the context” specifically “for generalizing to longer contexts” (16k-256k tokens) — a context-window extension architecture, not cross-session persistence (T4/E1).

The document explicitly states “No memory architecture... or integration recipe is disclosed” — a doctrinal/legal-style specification about memory “admissibility” with no memory mechanism proposed or evaluated (T5).

ActionEngine's “Crawling Agent... constructs an updatable state-machine memory of the GUIs through offline exploration” and “execution failures trigger a... fallback that repairs the failed action and updates the memory” — the agent writes and repairs its own memory (T2).

MERIT “maintains an online dual-polarity memory of oracle-verified corrections and observed unsuccessful directions” where “only memories from earlier finalized episodes are eligible for retrieval” (T2).
“we provide a review of the current efforts to develop LLM agents... we examine the memory management approaches used in these agents” — an explicit review (D1/E4).

SmartVector uses “a background consolidation agent [that] detects contradictions, builds dependency edges, and propagates updates along those edges” within a RAG embedding store — run-time writes added to a retrieval pipeline (T2).

GPM is “an auditable bitemporal state-transition model with source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release” for long-horizon agent memory (T2).

SkillComposer “predict[s] an executable skill plan” by selecting/ordering from “a real, human-curated skill library” — composition over a pre-existing curated library, with no description of the agent authoring new memory entries at run time (T2/E3).

NaQ is “a data augmentation strategy that transforms standard video-text narrations into training data for a video query localization model” on Ego4D — a supervised video-language grounding method with no LLM-based agent described (D2/E6).

“The present survey examines the role of big data analytics in advancing remote sensing and geospatial analysis”, with LSTM as one of several ML techniques — an explicit survey unrelated to agent memory (D1/E4).

H2M2 proposes “an asymmetric memory architecture consisting of capacity-centric and bandwidth-centric memory” for GPU LLM inference — a hardware memory management paper, not cross-turn agent state (T1/E1).

“LLM-powered agents, equipped with profile and memory modules, simulate the forgery creation process” — memory is named only as one equipped module, never elaborated or evaluated; the contribution is the forgery-data generation/detection pipeline (T5).

The position paper argues “we must augment LLMs with semantic memory and associative learning systems. By adopting a modular architecture that decouples these cognitive functions” — a primary proposal (D1) for external memory augmentation; mechanism detail is thin, so included per the uncertainty rule.

The paper specifies invariants for “organisational agent memory”, including “existence-oracle-free cross-node recall” and “contradiction-preserving attributed organisational memory” — a primary specification squarely about memory-system properties (T6).
ES-MemEval “systematically evaluates five core memory capabilities: information extraction, temporal reasoning, conflict detection, abstention, and user modeling” for conversational agents (T6).

Ensemble QSP's “three-layer hierarchical memory architecture... keeps injected context bounded and constant... by capping each state category and evicting completed work” for long-horizon multi-agent modeling (T4).
StructMemEval “tests the agent's ability to organize its long-term memory, not just factual recall” — a benchmark for agent memory structure (T6).
MEM1 “updates a compact shared internal state that jointly supports memory consolidation and reasoning... strategically discarding irrelevant or redundant information” across multi-turn tasks (T4).

Back-Reveal shows a “backdoored agent invokes memory-access tool calls to retrieve stored user context and exfiltrates it via disguised retrieval tool calls” — an extraction attack on agent session memory (T6).

SF-AMS “replaces static retrieval and heuristic decay with a utility-driven survival mechanism that updates memory importance from usage redundancy and temporal signals, inducing a hierarchical memory structure” (T4).

The study measures human “long-term retention of productive vocabulary” after using an LLM chatbot for language learning — human learner memory, with no agent-authored memory mechanism described (T5).

MAIN-RAG has “multiple LLM agents collaboratively filter and score retrieved documents” pulled from external retrieval each query, with no persistent store the agents write to across turns — a classical RAG filtering improvement (T2/E3).

MAPLE decomposes into “Memory handles storage and retrieval infrastructure; Learning extracts intelligence from accumulated interactions asynchronously; Personalization applies learned knowledge in real-time” (T2).

BMAM “decomposes memory into episodic, semantic, salience-aware, and control-oriented components” and “organizes episodic memories along explicit timelines and retrieves evidence by fusing multiple complementary signals” (T2).
Same “PerLTQA” dataset/authors as record 15994 (“Memory Classification, Retrieval, and Synthesis” vs. “...and Fusion”) — a duplicate of another record in this batch (D3/E7).
“This survey carefully analyzes 72 studies on LLM-based medical agents... and systematically introduces a structured taxonomy” — an explicit survey (D1/E4).

EVAF performs “parametric writes” (LoRA consolidation) into “a small parametric store” while the study frames this as “distinct from and complementary to retrieval access” against a maintained index — an ambiguous parametric/external-store hybrid, included per the T3 uncertainty rule.

MemSecBench is “a task-grounded benchmark for the lifecycle security of agent memory systems” tracking “malicious memory persists” through a “Write–Execute–Forget protocol” — an attack/security benchmark for agent memory (T6).
FinPerMA is “an event-grounded benchmark that evaluates personalized memory against frozen longitudinal investor trajectories” for LLM agents (T6).
